title: Simplex descent for relative marked mapping quasicategories
statement:
Use small simplicial sets, quasicategories and coherent functor categories of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], and marked simplicial sets and relative cocartesian equivalences of [lem-coef-marked-relative-cartesian-model]. Fix a small quasicategory $S$. For a marked simplicial set $(X,M_X)$ over $S$, and a cocartesian fibration $q:Z\to S$ marked by all its cocartesian edges, let $\mathcal F_S(X,Z)$ have $k$-simplices the maps $a:X\times\Delta^k\to Z$ over $S$ such that, at every vertex $v$ of $\Delta^k$, $a|_{X\times\{v\}}$ takes $M_X$ to cocartesian edges. Operators act by restriction in the parameter. These are quasicategories, including all transformations over $S$ between their vertex maps.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a marked map over $S$, with no fibrancy or injectivity assumption on $X,Y$ or $f$. Assume that for every $n\geq0$ and simplex $\sigma:\Delta^n\to S$, its marked pullback $f_\sigma:X\times_S\Delta^n\to Y\times_S\Delta^n$ is a weak equivalence in the relative cocartesian model structure over $\Delta^n$. Then $f$ is a relative cocartesian weak equivalence over $S$, and for every cocartesian fibration $Z\to S$ restriction is an equivalence of the entire quasicategories
$$f^*:\mathcal F_S(Y,Z)\xrightarrow{\simeq}\mathcal F_S(X,Z).$$
The comparison is the simplicial precomposition map; its parameter simplices are not required to be equivalences. The assertions are universe-relative, and remain valid after enlarging the universe. No assumption that the simplex category of $S$ is finite is made.

source.place: HTT Proposition 3.1.3.3 (cocartesian dual) for the marked mapping-object criterion; Proposition 3.1.3.7 and the skeletal gluing argument of Proposition 3.2.2.8 for simplex descent, in the marked relative model. The marked descent formulation is agent-formulated from those model-category results, not a verbatim statement of 3.2.2.8 (which concerns underlying categorical equivalences). Read online. WANTED: local archive of HTT. No matching Stacks tag.

proof.text:
Write $\mathsf M_S^{\mathrm{co}}$ for the cocartesian relative marked model category. Its cofibrations are monomorphisms, every object is cofibrant, and its fibrant objects are the naturally marked cocartesian fibrations. Use the opposite of the relative marked lifting calculus whenever it is stated in cartesian form. Opposite reverses the simplex order; the order-reversing identification $[n]^{\mathrm{op}}\cong[n]$ identifies the opposite of a standard simplex, its boundary, and its flat or sharp marking with the corresponding standard object. It also preserves products and colimits. More precisely, applying opposite to a parameterized map gives $\operatorname{Map}^{\epsilon}_{S^{\mathrm{op}}}(U^{\mathrm{op}},(Z^{\mathrm{op}})^
atural)\cong(\operatorname{Map}^{\epsilon}_S(U,Z^
atural))^{\mathrm{op}}$ for $\epsilon= lat,\sharp$; inner-horn fillers, Kan fillers and the inverse-triangle definition of equivalence edges are preserved by reversal. In particular the opposite lifting calculus says that $\operatorname{Map}^{ lat}_S(U,Z^
atural)$ is a quasicategory for every marked source $U$, and its sharp mapping complex is its core. A marked map $U	imes(\Delta^k)^ lat	o Z^
atural$ is exactly a map whose restrictions at every parameter vertex preserve the marked edges of $U$: a marked product edge has a constant second coordinate. Thus $\mathcal F_S(U,Z)=\operatorname{Map}^{ lat}_S(U,Z^
atural)$, with precisely the operators and unrestricted parameter simplices in the statement.

source.place: Remark 3.1.3.1 and Remark 3.1.3.9; identify the flat mapping object

proof.text: For a simplex $\sigma:\Delta^n\to S$, composition with $\sigma$ is a left Quillen functor $\sigma_!: \mathsf M_{\Delta^n}^{\mathrm{co}}\to\mathsf M_S^{\mathrm{co}}$. A left Quillen functor preserves weak equivalences between cofibrant objects, and all marked objects here are cofibrant. Consequently the assumed weak equivalence $f_\sigma$ is also a weak equivalence when its source and target are regarded simply as objects over $S$. In the remainder of the descent argument all weak equivalences and all colimits are in the one model category $\mathsf M_S^{\mathrm{co}}$. In particular no pullback functor is being assumed to preserve arbitrary weak equivalences.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.3.7 and base-composition Quillen adjunction; setup for the gluing argument of Proposition 3.2.2.8

proof.text:
For any small simplicial set $T\to S$ put $X_T=X\times_S T$ and $Y_T=Y\times_S T$, with the inherited markings and maps to $S$. The boundary-cell decomposition gives $T^{(-1)}=\varnothing$ and $T^{(n)}$, its $n$-skeleton, with union $T$. Let $I_n$ be the set of nondegenerate $n$-simplices $\tau:\Delta^n\to T$. There is a pushout
$$T^{(n)}=T^{(n-1)}\amalg_{\coprod_{\tau\in I_n}\partial\Delta^n}\coprod_{\tau\in I_n}\Delta^n.$$
Pulling these pieces back to $X$ gives the marked pushout
$$X_{T^{(n)}}=X_{T^{(n-1)}}\amalg_{\coprod_{\tau\in I_n}X_{\partial\Delta^n}}\coprod_{\tau\in I_n}X_{\Delta^n},$$
where each factor is pulled back using $\tau$ and $T\to S$; the same formula holds for $Y$. To check the identity, in each degree represent an element of the base pushout by a simplex in one of its pieces and keep its fixed $X$-coordinate; the identifications are exactly those on the common boundary. Use the explicit marked-pushout convention of [def-coef-infinity-marked-coanodyne]. An edge of any such piece is marked precisely when its $X$-coordinate is marked, so this bijection and its inverse preserve markings, including the quotient markings of the pushout. The boundary-to-simplex maps and the skeleton inclusions remain monomorphisms after pullback. The same degreewise description gives $X_T=\operatorname{colim}_{n\geq0}X_{T^{(n)}}$ and the corresponding formula for $Y$.

source.place: Proposition 3.2.2.8, degreewise base-change pushout identities; boundary-cell decomposition

proof.text: Prove simultaneously for all maps $T\to S$ that $f_T:X_T\to Y_T$ is a weak equivalence whenever $T$ has dimension at most $n$. For $n=-1$ both objects are empty and the map is the identity. Suppose the assertion is known in dimension at most $n-1$ and let $\dim T\leq n$. In the two pushout spans of Step 3, the comparison at $T^{(n-1)}$ is a weak equivalence by induction. Each boundary comparison is one by induction too, since $\partial\Delta^n$ has dimension $n-1$, with $\partial\Delta^0=\varnothing$. Each simplex comparison is one by Step 2 applied to the composite $\Delta^n\to T\to S$. Part (a) of the cofibrant colimit comparison makes the two coproduct comparisons weak equivalences. All six objects in the resulting map of spans are cofibrant; both boundary-to-simplex coproduct maps are cofibrations. Part (b) therefore makes the pushout comparison $f_T$ a weak equivalence. This proves the induction, including arbitrary sets $I_n$ and the empty set. The boundary-to-old-skeleton map need not be injective, and no injectivity of $f$ is used.

source.place: Proposition 3.2.2.8, induction on cells, applied in the relative marked model; cofibrant colimit comparison (a),(b)

proof.text: For an arbitrary small $T\to S$, every $T^{(n)}$ has finite dimension, so Step 4 applies to $f_{T^{(n)}}$. The skeleton inclusions give cofibration sequences of cofibrant objects on both sides by Step 3. Apply part (c) of the cofibrant colimit comparison to the ordinal $\omega$: there are no nonzero limit stages below $\omega$ to check, and the initial objects $X_{T^{(0)}}$ and $Y_{T^{(0)}}$ are cofibrant. The degreewise colimit identities of Step 3 now imply that $f_T$ is a weak equivalence in $\mathsf M_S^{\mathrm{co}}$. Take $T=S$ with the identity base map to conclude that $f$ is a relative cocartesian weak equivalence. Neither a finite simplex category nor a general filtered-colimit theorem for this model structure was used.

source.place: Proposition 3.2.2.8, passage from skeleta to the entire base; cofibrant colimit comparison (c)

proof.text: Use the coanodyne class of [def-coef-infinity-marked-coanodyne]: a marked map is coanodyne exactly when its opposite is marked anodyne. Take the opposite of the functorial relative marked-anodyne replacement to obtain $i_U:U\to RU$ over $S$ for every marked $U$, with $RU$ a naturally marked cocartesian fibration. Each $i_U$ is coanodyne and a trivial cofibration in $\mathsf M_S^{\mathrm{co}}$. Functoriality gives $Rf:RX\to RY$ and $Rf\,i_X=i_Y f$. By Step 5 and two-out-of-three $Rf$ is a weak equivalence. The fibrant-object inverse criterion in the relative model theorem supplies a marked map $r:RY\to RX$ over $S$ and paths $rRf\simeq1_{RX}$ and $Rf r\simeq1_{RY}$ in the appropriate relative sharp mapping Kan complexes.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.3.5 and Proposition 3.1.4.1, cocartesian dual; functorial naturally marked replacement

proof.text:
Fix the test cocartesian fibration $Z\to S$. If $i:U\to V$ is coanodyne, restriction $i^*:\mathcal F_S(V,Z)\to\mathcal F_S(U,Z)$ lifts every simplicial boundary inclusion. Indeed a lifting problem against $\partial\Delta^k\hookrightarrow\Delta^k$ is, by the flat mapping adjunction from Step 1, a marked lifting problem over $S$ against
$$ (V\times(\partial\Delta^k)^\flat)\amalg_{U\times(\partial\Delta^k)^\flat}(U\times(\Delta^k)^\flat)\longrightarrow V\times(\Delta^k)^\flat.$$
The opposite marked-anodyne pushout-product theorem makes this map coanodyne. The opposite relative lifting criterion for $Z^\natural\to S^\sharp$ fills the problem. This includes $k=0$ and hence surjectivity on vertices. To pass from boundaries to an arbitrary monomorphism of simplicial sets, use its boundary-cell decomposition: choose lifts on the coproduct of new cells at each stage, retaining the already prescribed boundary values, and take their union at the limit. Hence $i^*$ has right lifting against every monomorphism. The Joyal model structure identifies such maps with trivial fibrations, so $i^*$ is a Joyal weak equivalence. Its two objects are quasicategories by Step 1, and the Joyal quasicategory characterization makes it a coherent functor equivalence. Apply this in particular to $i_X$ and $i_Y$.

source.place: Remark 3.1.3.4, the flat-boundary pushout-product lifting argument, cocartesian dual

proof.text: Put $A=\mathcal F_S(RX,Z)$ and $B=\mathcal F_S(RY,Z)$. Precomposition with the marked inverse $r:RY\to RX$ of Step 6 gives $r^*:A\to B$. For each sharp edge $H_X$ in the path from $rRf$ to $1_{RX}$, apply [lem-cbc-marked-homotopy-precomposition] with $U=V=RX$, $W=Z$ and $H=H_X$. It gives a simplicial transformation between the corresponding precomposition endofunctors of $A$, with component $aH_X$ at every vertex $a:RX\to Z$. Apply the same lemma with $U=V=RY$, $W=Z$ and each edge $H_Y$ of the other sharp path to obtain transformations on $B$ with components $bH_Y$. The lemma applies because each edge in these paths is a marked map with sharp parameter over $S$, and hence also with flat parameter. Its formula retains all parameter simplices of $A$ and $B$.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.3.5, strong inverse data; Remark 3.1.3.1; the pointwise natural-equivalence test is Kerodon Theorem 4.4.4.4, Tag 01DK

proof.text: For each transformation just constructed, its vertex components are sharp mapping edges by [lem-cbc-marked-homotopy-precomposition]. The opposite relative marked lifting calculus identifies the sharp mapping complexes into $Z^\natural$ with the cores of $A$ and $B$. Thus all those components are equivalence edges. Apply [lem-coef-infinity-pointwise-equivalences] with $(K,\mathcal C)=(A,A)$ and $(B,B)$ respectively: each transformation is an equivalence edge in its functor simplicial set. The objects $A,B$ are quasicategories by Step 1, and their functor simplicial sets are quasicategories by [lem-coef-joyal-homotopy-exponentials].

source.place: Proposition 3.1.3.5, strong inverse data; Remark 3.1.3.1; the pointwise natural-equivalence test is Kerodon Theorem 4.4.4.4, Tag 01DK

proof.text: The endpoint identities in [lem-cbc-marked-homotopy-precomposition] identify the resulting chains in $\operatorname{Fun}(A,A)$ and $\operatorname{Fun}(B,B)$ as chains from $(Rf)^*r^*$ to $1_A$ and from $r^*(Rf)^*$ to $1_B$. To replace each chain by one equivalence edge, use [lem-coef-infinity-mapping-composition] in these functor quasicategories: every edge has a class in the ordinary homotopy category, equivalence edges have precisely invertible classes, and each component class is represented by an edge. Compose the classes, inverting any backwards edge. Their composite is invertible and therefore has an equivalence-edge representative with the required endpoints. For a length-zero chain use the identity edge. These two coherent natural equivalences exhibit $(Rf)^*$ and $r^*$ as inverse functor equivalences by [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones].

source.place: Proposition 3.1.3.5, strong inverse data; Remark 3.1.3.1; the pointwise natural-equivalence test is Kerodon Theorem 4.4.4.4, Tag 01DK

proof.text: Precomposition and $Rf\,i_X=i_Y f$ give the strictly commuting square whose top map is $(Rf)^*:\mathcal F_S(RY,Z)\to\mathcal F_S(RX,Z)$, bottom map is $f^*:\mathcal F_S(Y,Z)\to\mathcal F_S(X,Z)$, and vertical maps are $i_Y^*$ and $i_X^*$. The top is a coherent functor equivalence by Steps 8-10, and the vertical maps are such equivalences by Step 7. Regard these as Joyal weak equivalences by the quasicategory characterization. Two-out-of-three applied to the two equal composites makes $f^*$ a Joyal weak equivalence, and the same characterization makes this specified simplicial precomposition map a coherent functor equivalence. This proves the entire mapping-quasicategory assertion, rather than only its assertion about cores.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.3.3, equivalence on flat mapping objects, established here via naturally marked replacements

proof.text: All indexing sets $I_n$, the countable skeleton sequence, degreewise constructions, and functorial marked replacements lie in the universe of the input. To check compatibility with a larger universe, use the same replacements and $Rf$. The small marked inverse $r$ and its sharp homotopies from Step 6 are still inverse data there. The same small coanodyne replacement maps are still trivial cofibrations: their opposite marked-anodyne cell presentations remain such presentations in the larger universe, where those same generating maps are allowed. The relative model inverse criterion and two-out-of-three consequently show that a small relative weak equivalence remains one after enlargement; the converse follows by restricting the class of test fibrations. Steps 7-11 then apply also to test cocartesian fibrations $Z$ from the larger universe. In particular the same simplicial precomposition comparison has the required meaning in every containing universe.

source.place: Universe-relative constructions in Sections 3.1.1-3.1.4; small inverse witnesses and marked cell presentations

proof_origin.place: Agent-formulated marked analogue of the skeletal gluing proof of Proposition 3.2.2.8, using existing general model colimit nodes. The full mapping-object argument is written out from Remark 3.1.3.4 and Proposition 3.1.3.5; it proves the criterion of Proposition 3.1.3.3 without adding that criterion as a new node.
